html:
Joan of Arc was a French peasant girl who, saying that saints had told her to save France, led troops in the Hundred Years' War and helped turn it against England. She was captured, tried for heresy and burned at Rouen in 1431, aged about 19.

She was born around 1412 in Domrémy, in eastern France. At that time England and its ally Burgundy held Paris and much of the north, and the French heir, Charles, had not even been crowned. In 1429 Joan, then about 17, persuaded Charles to send her with an army to the siege of Orléans. The English lifted the siege within days of her arrival.

What followed:

  • More victories along the Loire, then a march to Reims, where Charles was crowned as Charles VII in July 1429, with Joan beside him.
  • A failed attack on Paris that autumn.
  • Capture by the Burgundians at Compiègne in May 1430; they sold her to the English.

A church court at Rouen, run by clergy loyal to England, tried her for heresy, using among other charges her wearing of men's clothes. She was burned on 30 May 1431. Twenty five years later a retrial ordered by the Pope cleared her name. France won the war in 1453.

She became a national symbol, claimed by royalists, republicans and nationalists alike. The Catholic Church made her a saint in 1920, and she is one of the patron saints of France.
